clue.text: There may be a dramatic scene between this couple

definitions.text: There may be a dramatic scene between this couple

blocks.clueFragment: There may be a dramatic scene between this couple
blocks.note: surface reading: two partners whose relationship produces theatrical rows
setter's reading: a pair of stage drapes, with a scene of a play performed in the gap between them

explanation.walkthrough: 'Couple' and 'dramatic scene' suggest a squabbling pair of people; the pair is really two pieces of fabric on a stage, opening on to a scene of the drama.
explanation.definitionFit: Theatre stages traditionally have a pair of drapes that part to reveal each scene of the play.

clue.text: A world-renowned old red shed men put up

indicators.note: in a down clue, putting something up raises it, so the letters read from bottom to top

blocks.note: to cast is to shed, as a snake casts its skin
OR, other ranks, is the usual abbreviation for soldiers who are not officers

explanation.surface: Someone has a famous old red shed that some workmen erected.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Red' looks like the colour of the shed, but it means a communist; only the men are turned up, so the shedding word stays as it is.
explanation.definitionFit: Fidel Castro, the Cuban revolutionary leader, was a famous communist, and a Red is crossword shorthand for a communist.

clue.text: Gathering to consume drug? Honestly!

indicators.note: consuming something takes it inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: a rally is a mass gathering of people
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: A shocked onlooker exclaims about a party where people take drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark belongs to the definition: both words are cries of disbelief or exasperation.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are interjections expressing exasperation or disbelief, as in 'Really, what a thing to do!'

clue.text: Exceptional to get out of head with joints

indicators.note: getting something out of the head removes it from the very top, so the opening letter goes

blocks.note: particular can mean special or exceptional, as in 'of particular interest'

explanation.surface: Something remarkable gets you high when smoked in joints.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of head' and 'joints' suggest getting stoned; the head is the first letter of the long word for exceptional.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective is the anatomical term for things relating to or having articulations, the joints of the body.

clue.text: A reason we got drunk with gin drink

indicators.note: drunk letters stagger out of their order and end up rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone explains why a group got drunk on gin and a mixer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drink' seems to be another alcoholic beverage, but in crosswords 'the drink' is the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: The drink is informal slang for the sea or ocean, and this is a stretch of the North Atlantic off Norway's coast.

clue.text: I don’t know you primarily process refuse

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only the opening letter is wanted

blocks.note: what a quiz contestant says when they cannot answer
U stands for you in text speak
the first letter of process

explanation.surface: Someone admits they have no idea how to handle waste disposal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refuse' reads as rubbish to be processed, but it is the verb meaning to decline.
explanation.definitionFit: To let an opportunity go by is to decline it, the verb sense of turning something down.

clue.text: Familiar with a motorway journey

blocks.note: taken as written
the M1, Britain's main north-south motorway from London, read with the 1 as the letter I
to go is to journey or travel

explanation.surface: Someone is well acquainted with driving along a motorway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Familiar' looks like an adjective meaning well known, but it is the noun for a close friend. The M1 is the London-to-Yorkshire motorway, and setters often treat its 1 as an I.
explanation.definitionFit: A familiar is an intimate companion, and the Spanish word for a friend is used informally in English.

clue.text: Work outfit edged stone slab up my street

indicators.note: to edge something here is to trim its edges, so both outer letters are cut away

blocks.note: a suit is what an office worker wears
a tablet is a flat slab of stone bearing an inscription

explanation.surface: Someone in work clothes is laying edging stones on a slab in the road where they live.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up' seems to describe the slab, but it starts the idiom that defines the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Something up your street suits your tastes or abilities, so the idiom means fitting or appropriate.

clue.text: How a hit-maker might be paid is improper

definitions.text: How a hit-maker might be paid

blocks.clueFragment: How a hit-maker might be paid
blocks.note: first meaning, read as two words: a songwriter could be paid for each stanza written
second meaning: contrary, wrong-headed or unacceptable

explanation.surface: The way a pop songwriter is remunerated turns out to be unfair.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half is a whimsical definition: split the answer as PER VERSE and it describes payment by the stanza.
explanation.definitionFit: Perverse means contrary to what is right or acceptable, which fits improper behaviour.

clue.text: Model-type encircled by gawpers and cranks?

indicators.note: something encircled is ringed round, so one piece sits inside another

blocks.note: people who gawp are people who stare
the Model T was Ford's famous early car, so the type of Model is T

explanation.surface: A fashion model is surrounded by gawking oddballs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cranks' looks like eccentrics among the gawpers, but it is the verb: things that crank engines into life. The question mark flags this definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Starter motors and old starting handles turn an engine over, which is what cranking an engine means.

clue.text: One had to intervene in row to make it more orderly

indicators.note: to intervene is to come between, so one piece goes into the middle of another

blocks.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
'd is the contracted form of had, as in I'd
a tier is a row, as of seats

explanation.surface: Someone had to step into an argument to calm things down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' suggests a quarrel, but it is a line of seats.
explanation.definitionFit: The comparative of tidy describes something neater and better arranged than before.

clue.text: Fantastic rooms heir had in piles

indicators.note: something fantastic is fanciful and unreal, so these letters are reimagined in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An heir lived in splendid rooms in his stately homes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piles' looks like grand country houses, which suits the rooms and the heir; it is the medical complaint.
explanation.definitionFit: Piles is the everyday name for swollen veins around the anus, the condition doctors call by the longer word.

clue.text: Remains in middle of Area 51 close to disc

indicators.note: the middle of a word is its central letters, so only those are kept
the close of something is its end, so only the final letter is used

blocks.note: the two central letters of Area
LI is 51 in Roman numerals
the final letter of disc

explanation.surface: Alien remains lie at the heart of Area 51, near where a flying saucer crashed.
explanation.walkthrough: Area 51 is the secret US base linked with UFO legends, so 'disc' feels like a flying saucer.
explanation.definitionFit: A relic is an object surviving from the past, something left behind, which is what remains are.

clue.text: Fancy Truss U-turned over judge

indicators.note: making a U-turn means heading back the way you came, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: a truss is a bundle of hay or straw, as is a bale
O is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for an over
to rate is to judge or assess

explanation.surface: Imagine former Prime Minister Liz Truss reversing her policy on the judiciary.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital T makes Truss the short-lived Prime Minister famous for U-turns; here it is just a bundle of hay.
explanation.definitionFit: Fancy as an adjective describes something ornate and intricate, highly detailed rather than plain.

clue.text: Criminal selling amber sculptures

indicators.note: a criminal act bends the rules, so the letters break from their order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone dealing in stolen amber carvings is breaking the law.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface nods at the long dispute over whether Lord Elgin's removal of these carvings from Athens was legitimate.
explanation.definitionFit: They are classical Greek marble friezes and statues from the Parthenon, now displayed in the British Museum.

clue.text: Change positions in bottom class

blocks.note: the rear is the bottom, the backside
a range is a class or series of products

explanation.surface: Pupils swap seats in the lowest set at school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottom class' reads as one phrase about a school stream, but the two words are separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: To put things in a different order is to alter where each one stands, moving them around.

clue.text: Song about extremely venerable old lady

definitions.text: Song about extremely venerable old lady

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece wraps the others
the extremes of a word are its outermost letters, so only those are taken

blocks.note: an aria is a song in an opera
the first and last letters of venerable
one's old lady is one's mother, Ma

explanation.surface: A hymn is written about a very revered woman.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: the prayer set to music addresses the Virgin Mary, the most venerated of women.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin prayer Hail Mary has famous musical settings by Schubert and Bach-Gounod, honouring the mother of Jesus.

clue.text: Weapon head of teaching found in new toilets

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, so just that is kept
a new version is a remade one, so these letters take a fresh order
something found in another is inside it, so one piece is placed within

blocks.note: the first letter of teaching
taken as written

explanation.surface: A headteacher discovers a weapon hidden in the school's newly built toilets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' sits after the word it scrambles, so it reads as an adjective for the lavatories.
explanation.definitionFit: A stiletto is a short dagger with a slender tapering blade, a classic weapon of assassins.

clue.text: Animal bones found in America

blocks.note: surface reading: skeletons of creatures dug up in the United States, perhaps fossils
setter's reading: Bones is the nickname of the Star Trek doctor, so an animal Bones is an animal doctor, called by the long title in American usage

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bones' is slang for a doctor, from Dr McCoy in Star Trek; Britons shorten the animal doctor's title, while Americans use the full form.
explanation.definitionFit: An animal doctor is formally a practitioner of veterinary medicine, and the full word is standard American usage for one.

clue.text: Bands Peel originally supported

indicators.note: originally points to the origin, the very start, so the first letter is taken

blocks.note: to peel something is to strip it
the first letter of supported

explanation.surface: The late DJ John Peel was the first to back many groups.
explanation.walkthrough: John Peel was a BBC radio DJ famous for championing new bands, so 'Bands' looks like groups he backed rather than lengths of material.
explanation.definitionFit: Long narrow pieces of material, such as strips of cloth, are also called bands.

clue.text: Mean to accept old fine? Certainly not

indicators.note: accepting something takes it in, so one piece is held inside another

blocks.note: near is an old-fashioned word for stingy or mean with money
O is the standard abbreviation for old
F is the abbreviation for fine, as on pencil leads

explanation.surface: Would a stingy person agree to pay an old penalty? Never.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fine' looks like a penalty, which suits a miser; it is just its abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: The British colloquial exclamation is an emphatic refusal, meaning there is no chance at all.

clue.text: Choppers clandestinely paid for in cash

definitions.text: Choppers clandestinely paid for in cash

blocks.clueFragment: Choppers clandestinely paid for in cash
blocks.note: surface reading: helicopters or axes bought secretly with untraceable money
setter's reading: choppers is slang for teeth, and the tooth fairy secretly leaves coins under a child's pillow for each one that falls out

explanation.walkthrough: 'Choppers' suggests helicopters in a shady deal; it is slang for teeth, and the secret buyer is the tooth fairy.
explanation.definitionFit: A child's first set of teeth falls out naturally, and folklore says the tooth fairy pays money for each one.

clue.text: Cloth one royal put in Edwardian dresser?

indicators.note: putting something in places it inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: a Ted, or Teddy boy, was a 1950s youth who wore Edwardian-style clothes
the royal we, where a monarch speaks of themself as we

explanation.surface: A member of the royal family fits fabric into an antique Edwardian chest of drawers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dresser' sounds like furniture but is a person who dresses in a certain style; Teddy boys were British youths of the 1950s.
explanation.definitionFit: Tweed is a rough woollen fabric, originally from Scotland, a classic cloth for jackets.

clue.text: Percentage of quota falling short

indicators.note: falling short means not reaching the end, so the final letter is lost

blocks.note: a fixed allowance, a quota

explanation.surface: A proportion of a target figure has not been met.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Percentage of quota' reads as one phrase, but the first word stands alone as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A percentage expresses a proportion between two quantities, which is a kind of relationship expressed as a fraction.

clue.text: Singer right to hug diplomat? On the contrary!

indicators.note: a hug wraps arms around someone, so one piece holds another inside

blocks.note: an informer is said to sing to the police, and is also called a rat
R is the abbreviation for right
HE, His Excellency, is the title of an ambassador

explanation.surface: Is it right for a vocalist to embrace an ambassador? Quite the opposite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the contrary!' looks like an instruction to reverse the wordplay, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb introduces a correction, as in 'not cold; rather, warm', so it means the opposite holds.

clue.text: Somebody well-built I locked in trunk?

indicators.note: something locked in is shut inside, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: a well-built person is big
an elephant's trunk is its nose
taken as written

explanation.surface: A burly person shut someone in the boot of a car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trunk' suggests a car boot or chest, but it is an elephant's nose.
explanation.definitionFit: A somebody is an important or influential person, and the informal phrase means a person of importance.

clue.text: When to provide a home for destitute ducks

indicators.note: giving a home to someone takes them in, so one piece lives inside another

blocks.note: as can mean when, as in 'as I left'
void means empty or wholly lacking, as the destitute are

explanation.surface: Someone asks when they should give shelter to some homeless waterfowl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ducks' seems to be the homeless birds, but it is the verb for dodging.
explanation.definitionFit: To duck something is to dodge or evade it, as you duck a question or responsibility.

clue.text: One who might value classes Sorbonne hosts

indicators.note: a host has guests inside, so the answer sits within the words

blocks.note: inside the letters spanning the two words

explanation.surface: A Paris university runs courses for someone training to appraise property.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sorbonne is the famous university in Paris, which makes 'classes' look like teaching sessions.
explanation.definitionFit: An assessor is a person who estimates the worth of property, for tax or insurance purposes.
